classes.name: Plant
classes.summary: Materials that come from plants: fruit, grain, wood, bast and leaf fibres, resins, and the cloth and paper made from them.

classes.name: Animal
classes.summary: Materials that come from animals: meat, fish, milk, eggs, hide and leather, hair and silk fibres, shell, horn and feather.

classes.name: Fungi and microbes
classes.summary: Materials that come from fungi and bacteria: mushrooms, yeasts and moulds, the ferments that they make, and gums that bacteria make.

classes.name: Mineral
classes.summary: Materials that come out of the ground and stay close to their natural state: stone, clay, sand, salt, ash, earth pigments and binders.

classes.name: Metal
classes.summary: Metal elements, the alloys made from them, and metals with a plated or enamelled surface.

classes.name: Ceramic and glass
classes.summary: Materials that fire changes for ever: clay bodies, glazes, slips, glass, vitreous enamel, brick and tile.

classes.name: Polymer
classes.summary: Long-chain materials that people make: plastics, synthetic and regenerated fibres, rubber, and the cloth and paint made from them.

classes.name: Composite
classes.summary: Materials made from two or more materials that keep their own identity: concrete, plaster, paint, laminates and fibre composites.

materials.name: Agar
materials.summary: A seaweed gel that sets firm and stays firm when warm; it allows a hot jelly.

materials.name: Sodium alginate
materials.summary: A salt from brown seaweed that sets in contact with calcium: the gel skin of spherification.

materials.name: Lecithin
materials.summary: An emulsifier from egg yolk or soy; it holds the light airs of the modernist kitchen.

materials.name: Kombu
materials.summary: Kelp dried in the sun; with katsuobushi it makes dashi, the base stock of Japan. Rich in glutamate.

materials.name: Cork
materials.summary: A bark used for the stoppers and lids of storage jars.

materials.name: Oilskin
materials.summary: Cloth soaked in linseed oil for sailors and fishermen; Helly Hansen sold oiled linen in Norway from 1877.

materials.name: Waxed cotton
materials.summary: A dense cotton with a paraffin-wax finish that replaced linseed oil; it does not go stiff in the cold. The cloth of the country jacket.

materials.name: Wine
materials.summary: For deglazing, braising and sauce reduction.

materials.name: Parquet
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of herringbone oak parquet

materials.name: Wood flooring
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of oak plank flooring

materials.name: Olive oil
materials.summary: The fat of the south: raw, for frying and for confit.

materials.name: Dashi
materials.summary: Stock of kombu and katsuobushi; its umami taught French chefs a lighter base.

materials.name: Vinegar
materials.summary: Wine or cider made sour by acetic bacteria; the sauce acid of the North.

materials.name: Banana
materials.summary: The long, curved fruit of the banana plant: a yellow peel around soft, sweet, starchy flesh. People eat it raw, fried, steamed or dried.

materials.name: Berries
materials.summary: Lingonberry, cloudberry, sea buckthorn, bilberry, raspberry and strawberry, wild or grown.

materials.name: Bitter orange
materials.summary: The orange of duck à l'orange and marmalade; the sweet orange came later, after 1500.

materials.name: Grape
materials.summary: Eaten fresh, dried, pressed for verjuice or made into wine.

materials.name: Lemon
materials.summary: The Arabs grew lemons in Sicily and Spain; the acid of fish dishes and sauces.

materials.name: Lime
materials.summary: The Spanish took limes to the Americas, where they cure ceviche.

materials.name: Orchard fruit
materials.summary: Apple, pear, quince, plum and cherry from orchards.

materials.name: Peach
materials.summary: The Romans called it the Persian apple; pêche Melba of 1893 used it.

materials.name: Plantain (cooking banana)
materials.summary: A starchy cooking banana. It is fried, boiled or steamed while green or ripe, and is a staple of West Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America.

materials.name: Tropical fruit
materials.summary: Pineapple, mango, passion fruit and papaya; Europe grew pineapples in hothouses from the 1700s.

materials.name: Verjuice
materials.summary: The sour juice of unripe grapes; the acid of the medieval sauce before lemon and vinegar.

materials.name: Yuzu
materials.summary: A sour aromatic citrus of Japan; French chefs took it up in the 1990s.

materials.name: Bread
materials.summary: Flat bread from about 14,000 years ago; the medieval kitchen thickened sauces with it and served food on trenchers.

materials.name: Maize
materials.summary: Domesticated from teosinte; nixtamalised with lime for masa. Columbus took it to Spain.

materials.name: Quinoa
materials.summary: The seed of the Andean highlands; it reached European shops only in the late twentieth century.

materials.name: Rice
materials.summary: Asian rice reached Spain with the Moors; paella and risotto came later. Short grain for sushi and risotto.

materials.name: Rye
materials.summary: A hardy grain of the cold north; the dark sour bread of Scandinavia, Germany and Russia.

materials.name: Wheat
materials.summary: Einkorn and emmer were sown in the Near East; bread wheat followed. Flour is the base of bread, pastry, roux and pasta.

materials.name: Coriander leaf
materials.summary: The leaf herb of Asian and Latin American cooking; the seed is a separate spice.

materials.name: Fines herbes
materials.summary: Parsley, chervil, chives and tarragon, chopped fine; the herb mix of the French kitchen.

materials.name: Tarragon
materials.summary: The herb of béarnaise sauce and of poulet à l'estragon.

materials.name: Thyme and bay
materials.summary: With parsley, the bouquet garni of stocks and braises.

materials.name: Wild plants and flowers
materials.summary: Foraged leaves, flowers, berries, moss and needles; the base of the foraging kitchen.

materials.name: Bobbin lace
materials.summary: Lace plaited from threads on many bobbins over a pattern on a pillow; Flanders and the Low Countries led it.

materials.name: Leavers lace
materials.summary: Machine lace from the Leavers frame; it made lace a cloth of the middle class and of lingerie.

materials.name: Needle lace
materials.summary: Lace built from buttonhole stitches with a needle; Venetian 'punto in aria' was the lace of the ruff and the collar.

materials.name: Rubberised cloth
materials.summary: Two cotton cloths glued with naphtha-dissolved rubber; the first waterproof coat cloth, and the name of the coat.

materials.name: Crepe rubber
materials.summary: Raw latex rolled into crinkled sheets for a soft, grippy sole; the sole of the desert boot and the creeper.

materials.name: Natural rubber
materials.summary: Latex from the rubber tree; the Olmec made rubber balls. Raw rubber goes soft in heat and hard in cold.

materials.name: Banana leaf
materials.summary: The large, waxy leaf of the banana plant. Cooks wrap food in it to steam or grill it, and in South India it is the plate.

materials.name: Pulses
materials.summary: Lentil, chickpea, bean and pea: the protein of the plant kitchen.

materials.name: Tofu
materials.summary: Curd of soy milk pressed into blocks; the protein of the Buddhist kitchen.

materials.name: Nuts and seeds
materials.summary: Almond, hazelnut, walnut, sesame and pumpkin seed; the almond milk of medieval Lent.

materials.name: Paper cord
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of a seat woven from paper cord

materials.name: Banana plant (Musa)
materials.summary: A large herb of the genus Musa. Its stem is a pseudostem of rolled leaf bases; it gives fruit, leaves and fibre.

materials.name: Abacá (Manila hemp)
materials.summary: The fibre of Musa textilis, also called Manila hemp. It is strong and resists salt water, so it makes rope, paper and woven hats.

materials.name: Banana fibre (bashōfu)
materials.summary: Fibre from the pseudostem of the banana plant. In Okinawa it is woven into bashōfu cloth.

materials.name: Cane and bamboo
materials.summary: Woven cane or bamboo for the overhead handles of teapots and kettles.

materials.name: Coir
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of a coir door mat

materials.name: Cotton
materials.summary: Cotton threads at Mehrgarh and cloth at Mohenjo-daro; Peru grew a second species from about 4500 BC.

materials.name: Flax (linen)
materials.summary: Linen cloth from flax is in Egyptian graves of about 5000 BC; dyed wild flax fibres from a cave in Georgia are about 30,000 years old.

materials.name: Hemp
materials.summary: Hemp cloth is in Chinese graves of the third millennium BC; Europe used it for sailcloth, rope and work clothes.

materials.name: Toquilla straw
materials.summary: Palm-leaf straw from Ecuador, hand-woven into the 'Panama' hat.

materials.name: Black pepper
materials.summary: The most traded spice of the ancient world; Rome bought it by the tonne.

materials.name: Chilli pepper
materials.summary: Capsicum went from the Americas round the world in fifty years: to Hungary, India, Sichuan and Korea.

materials.name: Cinnamon
materials.summary: Bark of the cinnamon tree; the base of the medieval cameline sauce.

materials.name: Clove
materials.summary: Dried flower buds from the Spice Islands; studs the onion of a classic stock.

materials.name: Cocoa
materials.summary: Ground cacao beans drunk with chilli; Europe added sugar.

materials.name: Ginger
materials.summary: A rhizome used dried in medieval Europe and fresh in Asia.

materials.name: Grains of paradise
materials.summary: A peppery seed from the Guinea coast; a medieval spice that nearly left the kitchen.

materials.name: Nutmeg and mace
materials.summary: Seed and aril of one tree; in béchamel and the medieval spice mix.

materials.name: Saffron
materials.summary: Stigmas of the crocus; it coloured medieval dishes gold. Used now in risotto and bouillabaisse.

materials.name: Vanilla
materials.summary: Totonac people cured the pod of an orchid; the hand pollination of 1841 by Edmond Albius made it a crop.

materials.name: Cane sugar
materials.summary: Crystal sugar reached Europe through the crusades; a costly spice until the plantations.

materials.name: Artichoke
materials.summary: Bred from the cardoon in Sicily and Naples; Catherine de' Medici took it to France.

materials.name: Asparagus
materials.summary: Cato described its culture; white asparagus is grown in the dark under earth.

materials.name: Cabbage
materials.summary: Kale, cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli are one species, bred in Europe.

materials.name: Carrot
materials.summary: Purple and yellow at first; the orange carrot was bred in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century.

materials.name: Garlic
materials.summary: Used raw, confit or roasted; the mark of Provençal and southern cooking.

materials.name: Leek
materials.summary: A soft onion for soups and vichyssoise; the white is the part used.

materials.name: Onion
materials.summary: The base of most savoury cooking, sweated, browned or raw.

materials.name: Potato
materials.summary: Thousands of Andean kinds; Parmentier made it French food after 1772. Pommes purée, frites and chuño.

materials.name: Root vegetables
materials.summary: Turnip, swede, celeriac, beetroot and parsnip: the winter store of the north.

materials.name: Young greens and shoots
materials.summary: Pea shoots, young leaves, wild garlic and small salad leaves picked young.

materials.name: Shallot
materials.summary: A mild onion of the French sauce: beurre blanc, béarnaise and bordelaise start with it.

materials.name: Tomato
materials.summary: Mattioli recorded the pomi d'oro in 1544; the first Italian tomato sauce recipe is of 1692.

materials.name: Ash timber
materials.summary: Pale, straight-grained hardwood that bends well after steaming. Coachbuilders and early car makers cut body frames from it.

materials.name: Burr walnut
materials.summary: The figured veneer of a walnut burr; the dashboard and door cappings of the luxury car cabin.

materials.name: Fumed oak
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of smoked oak plank floor

materials.name: Oak
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of oiled oak plank floor

materials.name: Oiled oak
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of oiled oak plank floor

materials.name: Timber decking
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of weathered ribbed timber decking

materials.name: Whitened oak
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of white-oiled oak plank floor

materials.name: Wood
materials.summary: Timber for lids, stands, frames and toilet seats.

materials.name: Oxford cloth
materials.summary: A basket weave with a soft hand; Scottish mills named shirtings after universities. The cloth of the button-down shirt.

materials.name: Corduroy
materials.summary: A weft-pile cloth with cut cords ('wales'); the cloth of country trousers and the 1970s jacket.

materials.name: Terry towelling
materials.summary: A loop-pile cloth that Henry Christy saw in Turkey and his mill made by machine; the cloth of robes and sweatbands.

materials.name: Calico
materials.summary: A plain cotton from the Malabar coast; England banned printed calico imports in 1700 and 1721 to protect wool and silk weavers.

materials.name: Cambric (batiste)
materials.summary: A fine, dense plain weave for shirts, collars, handkerchiefs and lingerie, named after the town of Cambrai.

materials.name: Canvas and duck
materials.summary: A heavy plain weave for sails, tents, work coats and the upper of the first sneakers.

materials.name: Elastic webbing
materials.summary: A narrow woven band with rubber or elastane core threads; it forms the waistband, the strap and the leg band. Thomas Hancock patented rubber elastic for garments in 1820.

materials.name: Gingham
materials.summary: A yarn-dyed check in white and one colour; the name comes from a Malay word for striped cloth.

materials.name: Glazed chintz
materials.summary: A printed or painted cotton with a glazed surface; the East India companies brought it to Europe in the 17th century.

materials.name: Linen
materials.photo_applied: a linen curtain panel, hung

materials.name: Linen cloth
materials.summary: The oldest cloth of dress; cool, crisp and quick to crease. Shirts, summer suits and underwear were linen until cotton took over.

materials.name: Muslin
materials.summary: A fine, open cotton of hand-spun yarn from Dhaka; the name comes from Mosul. It was the cloth of the Empire-line dress after 1795.

materials.name: Poplin
materials.summary: A plain weave with a fine weft rib; the name may come from 'papeline', the cloth of the papal town of Avignon. The cloth of the dress shirt.

materials.name: Seersucker
materials.summary: Two warps at different tension make puckered stripes that stand off the skin; the name comes from Persian 'milk and sugar'.

materials.name: Ventile
materials.summary: A dense weave of long-staple cotton that swells when wet and keeps out water; made for the immersion suits of RAF pilots.

materials.name: Chino twill
materials.summary: A light cotton twill of US army trousers in the Philippines; the name comes from the Chinese cloth. It went to the campus after 1945.

materials.name: Coutil
materials.summary: A dense cotton twill, often in a herringbone weave, that resists the pull of the bones; the standard cloth of corset bodies.

materials.name: Denim
materials.summary: A warp-faced twill with an indigo warp and a white weft; 'serge de Nîmes'. Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented the riveted work trouser in 1873.

materials.name: Khaki drill
materials.summary: A cotton twill dyed the colour of dust ('khaki' in Urdu) for the Corps of Guides; armies took it for field dress.

materials.name: Alpaca and vicuña
materials.summary: Andean weavers used alpaca and vicuña fibre in the Paracas textiles; vicuña is the finest animal fibre in commercial use.

materials.name: Cashmere
materials.summary: The down of the Changthangi goat, woven into Kashmir shawls; Europe took the shawl as fashion from about 1800.

materials.name: Human hair
materials.summary: Hair of a loved person, woven or set under glass in mourning and sentimental jewels of the 19th century. Mourning rings with hair are known from the 17th century.

materials.name: Merino wool
materials.summary: Spain bred the fine merino sheep from about the 14th century and banned its export until the 18th century.

materials.name: Mohair
materials.summary: The hair of the Angora goat; it gives a lustrous, springy yarn for suiting and knitwear.

materials.name: Silk
materials.summary: China reeled silk from the cocoon of Bombyx mori; Byzantium got silkworms in about AD 552.

materials.name: Wool
materials.summary: Sheep with a woolly fleece appear in Mesopotamia in the fourth millennium BC; before that, sheep had hair.
materials.photo_applied: a folded wool throw on a chair

materials.name: Butter
materials.summary: The fat of the northern French kitchen; it took the place of oil and lard in sauces after 1650.

materials.name: Cheese
materials.summary: Strainers with milk fat from about 5500 BC; Parmigiano, Comté and Gruyère are hard cheeses for cooking.

materials.name: Cream
materials.summary: Double cream and crème fraîche thicken and enrich the sauces of the classic kitchen.

materials.name: Hen egg
materials.summary: Binds, raises, thickens and emulsifies: the tool of mayonnaise, hollandaise, soufflé and custard.

materials.name: Lard
materials.summary: Rendered pork fat; the frying fat of medieval and peasant kitchens.

materials.name: Feather
materials.summary: Ostrich, egret and other plumes that trimmed the hat; the Victorian trade in plumes and whole birds led to the first bird-protection laws.

materials.name: Goose down
materials.summary: The under-plumage of geese, in quilted baffles; Eddie Bauer patented the quilted down jacket after a near-fatal fishing trip.

materials.name: Felt
materials.summary: A cloth of matted fibres with no weave; the Pazyryk graves held felt saddle cloths and hangings. The cloth of hats.

materials.name: Loden
materials.summary: A fulled and napped wool that sheds rain and wind; the coat cloth of the Alpine countries.

materials.name: Caviar
materials.summary: Salted sturgeon roe; a luxury of the Russian court and the French restaurant.

materials.name: Cod
materials.summary: Dried as stockfish and salted as klippfisk; traded from Lofoten through the Middle Ages.

materials.name: Salmon
materials.summary: Wild in rivers, then farmed after 1970; cured, smoked or cooked pink.

materials.name: Sole and flat fish
materials.summary: Dover sole, turbot and brill: the fish of the classic kitchen, poached, grilled or meunière.

materials.name: Tuna
materials.summary: Raw as sushi in Japan after the 1840s; the fat belly is toro.

materials.name: Game birds
materials.summary: Pheasant, partridge, woodcock and pigeon; the medieval feast added swan, heron and peacock.

materials.name: Venison
materials.summary: Red deer, roe deer and reindeer; hung, roasted and served with a sharp berry sauce.

materials.name: Horn
materials.summary: Animal horn, heated and pressed or carved; it takes a translucent, amber-like colour and was a main material of Art Nouveau combs and pendants.

materials.name: Whalebone (baleen)
materials.summary: Plates of baleen from whales; thin strips of it stiffened stays and corsets until spring steel and plastic replaced it.

materials.name: Calfskin
materials.summary: Fine, tight-grained leather from calves for dress shoes, gloves and small leather goods.

materials.name: Chrome-tanned leather
materials.summary: Hide tanned with chromium salts in hours, not months; Augustus Schultz made the process commercial in 1884. Most leather now is chrome tanned.

materials.name: Exotic skin
materials.summary: Crocodile, alligator, ostrich and lizard skin; trade in most species is under CITES control since 1975.

materials.name: Kidskin
materials.summary: Soft, thin goatskin for gloves, evening shoes and linings.

materials.name: Patent leather
materials.summary: Leather with a hard, high-gloss lacquer; the shoe of evening dress and the 1960s boot.

materials.name: Shearling
materials.summary: Sheepskin with the wool left on; the bomber jacket, the boot and the coat lining.

materials.name: Shell cordovan
materials.summary: Dense leather from the shell under the hide of a horse's rump; the cordwainers of Córdoba gave the trade its name.

materials.name: Suede
materials.summary: Leather with the flesh side napped; the name comes from 'gants de Suède', Swedish gloves.

materials.name: Vegetable-tanned leather
materials.summary: Hide tanned with bark tannins; a cowhide shoe from the Areni-1 cave is about 5,500 years old. It darkens and takes a patina.

materials.name: Beef
materials.summary: The fillet, the rib and the braising cuts; tournedos Rossini and boeuf bourguignon.

materials.name: Lamb
materials.summary: Saddle, rack and leg; the roast of spring.

materials.name: Pork
materials.summary: Fresh, salted and cured; lard is its fat.

materials.name: Veal
materials.summary: The meat of the calf and the bones of the white and brown stock.

materials.name: Tulle (bobbinet)
materials.summary: A hexagonal net from Heathcoat's bobbinet machine; the cloth of the veil, the petticoat and the tutu.

materials.name: Chicken
materials.summary: The capon and the Bresse chicken of the French kitchen.

materials.name: Duck
materials.summary: Breast cooked pink and legs as confit; Peking duck in China.

materials.name: Foie gras
materials.summary: Fattened goose or duck liver; a mark of the French luxury kitchen since the eighteenth century.

materials.name: Flat-weave rug
materials.photo_applied: a flat-weave wool rug on a floor

materials.name: Hand-woven wool rug
materials.photo_applied: a hand-woven wool rug on a floor

materials.name: Conch shell
materials.summary: The pink and white layers of the conch shell, carved as a cameo; popular in Victorian jewellery. Italian carvers cut shell cameos from the 16th century.

materials.name: Cultured pearl
materials.summary: A pearl grown around a nucleus that a person put in the oyster; it made the pearl necklace a jewel of the middle class.

materials.name: Natural pearl
materials.summary: A pearl that grew in an oyster with no help; the most costly jewel of the court era.

materials.name: Tortoiseshell
materials.summary: The shell of the hawksbill turtle for combs, frames and boxes; CITES ended the trade, and acetate copies the pattern.

materials.name: Oyster
materials.summary: Sergius Orata farmed oysters at Baiae; eaten raw or poached.

materials.name: Sea urchin
materials.summary: Raw gonads, sweet and briny; uni in Japan.

materials.name: Shellfish
materials.summary: Lobster, langoustine, crab, scallop and prawn; the luxury of the coast.

materials.name: Honey
materials.summary: The sweetener of Europe before sugar.

materials.name: Aran knit
materials.summary: A thick cream knit of cables, diamonds and moss stitch; it became a fashion knit in the 1950s.

materials.name: Boiled wool
materials.summary: A wool knit that heat, water and rubbing shrink into a dense, felt-like cloth that does not fray; Tyrolean walk jackets were made of it, and Japanese designers of the 1980s used it for sculpted coats.

materials.name: Cashmere knit
materials.summary: A fine knit of cashmere down, the luxury form of knitwear; the fibre came to Europe in Kashmir shawls, and plain cashmere jumpers became a sign of quiet wealth.

materials.name: Fair Isle knit
materials.summary: A stranded knit in two colours each row; the Prince of Wales wore a Fair Isle jumper to golf in 1921.

materials.name: Frame-knit hosiery
materials.summary: Stockings from the knitting frame, the first textile machine of the modern kind; Nottingham became the centre of hosiery.

materials.name: Jersey
materials.summary: A plain weft knit from the island knitters; Gabrielle Chanel made wool jersey into women's dress in 1916.

materials.name: Brocade
materials.summary: A figured cloth with extra weft, often of metal thread, that floats on the face as a raised pattern; the cloth of court dress.

materials.name: Damask
materials.summary: A reversible figured cloth in which the pattern shows in satin on a ground of the opposite face; named after Damascus.

materials.name: Jacquard figured cloth
materials.summary: Cloth from a loom that lifts each warp thread by a punched card; the cards made large figured patterns cheap.

materials.name: Velvet
materials.summary: A warp-pile cloth with a short dense pile cut from a second warp; Italian cities wove it for courts and the church.

materials.name: Chiffon
materials.summary: A sheer, floating plain weave of highly twisted yarn for overlays, scarves and evening dress.

materials.name: Crêpe de Chine
materials.summary: A light silk with a pebbled surface from crepe-twisted weft; it drapes well on the bias.

materials.name: Taffeta
materials.summary: A crisp plain silk that rustles and holds a full skirt; the name comes from Persian 'taftah', twisted.

materials.name: Satin
materials.summary: A weave with long floats that gives a smooth, lustrous face; the name may come from Zaitun, the port of export.

materials.name: Flannel
materials.summary: A soft cloth that is napped after the weave; grey wool flannel became the suit and trouser cloth of the 20th century.

materials.name: Gabardine
materials.summary: A steep, tight twill of yarn proofed before the weave; it keeps out rain and lets the body breathe. The cloth of the trench coat.

materials.name: Harris Tweed
materials.summary: Hand-woven at home in the Outer Hebrides; the Orb mark dates from 1909 and an Act of Parliament protects the name since 1993.

materials.name: Houndstooth
materials.summary: A broken check from a 2/2 twill with four dark and four light yarns in warp and weft.

materials.name: Serge
materials.summary: A balanced twill with a clear diagonal rib, for uniforms, suits and coats.

materials.name: Silk twill
materials.summary: A fine, dense silk twill that takes a sharp print; it is the cloth of the printed square scarf and the necktie. Twill silk is in Chinese graves of the second century BC.

materials.name: Tartan
materials.summary: A twill check of coloured stripes in warp and weft; a check fragment from near Falkirk dates from about AD 250. The Dress Act of 1746 banned it in the Highlands.

materials.name: Tweed
materials.summary: A rough, thick twill of woollen yarn; the name comes from 'tweel', misread by a London merchant as the River Tweed.

materials.name: Worsted suiting
materials.summary: A smooth, firm cloth of combed long-staple yarn, named after the Norfolk village; the cloth of the tailored suit.

materials.name: Xanthan gum
materials.summary: A gum made by bacteria; a little thickens a sauce or holds a foam without heat.

materials.name: Miso
materials.summary: Soy paste fermented with koji; in soup, glazes and marinades.

materials.name: Soy sauce
materials.summary: Fermented soy beans and wheat. The Dutch East India Company shipped it from Nagasaki from 1647, and to Europe in the 1660s.

materials.name: Truffle
materials.summary: The black truffle of Périgord and the white truffle of Alba; shaved raw or cooked in sauce.

materials.name: Wild mushrooms
materials.summary: Ceps, morels, chanterelles; dried or fresh, foraged in the autumn and the spring.

materials.name: Liquid nitrogen
materials.summary: Nitrogen at minus 196 °C; it freezes ice cream in seconds and makes powders of fat.

materials.name: Coloured gemstone
materials.summary: Ruby, sapphire, emerald and the semi-precious stones: amethyst, citrine, turquoise, coral, onyx and others.

materials.name: Diamond
materials.summary: The hardest gem; Marcel Tolkowsky set the proportions of the round brilliant cut in 1919. The first diamond trade is in India, about 400 BC.

materials.name: Rock crystal
materials.summary: Clear quartz; it is cut, carved and engraved as a clear stone in jewels of many periods.

materials.name: Synthetic sapphire
materials.summary: Corundum grown by flame fusion; watch crystals use it because it scratches only under diamond.

materials.name: Quartz crystal
materials.summary: A slice of quartz that vibrates at a fixed rate when a current passes through it. It keeps the time in a quartz clock or watch.

materials.name: Jet
materials.summary: A black fossil wood that polishes to a deep shine; Queen Victoria's mourning after 1861 made it the jewel of grief.

materials.name: Luminous paint
materials.summary: Paint that glows in the dark. Radium salts gave the glow until the 1970s, then tritium, and from the middle 1990s strontium aluminate.

materials.name: Onyx
materials.summary: A banded black or white chalcedony; the black onyx band gave the hard contrast of Art Deco jewellery.

materials.name: Blued steel
materials.summary: Steel heated until a thin blue oxide forms on it; watchmakers use it for screws and hands. The blue is a heat colour, not a dye.

materials.name: Brass
materials.summary: A yellow alloy of copper and zinc for taps, fittings and frames.

materials.name: Cut steel
materials.summary: Small steel studs, faceted and riveted to a plate, that catch the light like diamonds; used in jewellery from the 18th century to the 1930s.

materials.name: Pinchbeck
materials.summary: A brass of copper and zinc that looks like gold; Georgian watch cases and jewellery used it.

materials.name: Pressed steel
materials.summary: Sheet steel pressed into body panels; the all-steel body replaced wood frames from the 1910s.

materials.name: Rose gold
materials.summary: Gold with copper for a pink tone, called 'Russian gold' in the 19th century; it came back in the 1940s and the 2010s.

materials.name: Spring steel
materials.summary: Tempered steel in thin flat strips; it gave corsets a bone that bends and returns, and it made the front busk. Steel mainsprings of clocks are known from the 15th century.

materials.name: Stainless steel
materials.summary: A corrosion-resistant steel for lids, frames and modern fittings.
materials.photo_applied: a brushed stainless steel worktop edge

materials.name: Steel
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of bare steel sheet with a mill finish

materials.name: Steel frame
materials.summary: The structural frame behind terracotta and faience cladding.

materials.name: Sterling silver
materials.summary: Silver of 925 parts in 1,000; England fixed the standard and the hallmark under Edward I in 1300.

materials.name: White gold
materials.summary: Gold with palladium or nickel, often plated with rhodium; a cheaper white metal than platinum after 1920.

materials.name: Yellow gold
materials.summary: Gold in carat alloys, from 9 to 22 carat; the base metal of jewellery and the dress watch case.

materials.name: Aluminium
materials.summary: A light metal, cheap after the electrolytic process of 1886; car bodies, trunks and watch cases use it.

materials.name: Copper
materials.summary: The first metal that people worked; it gave the rivet at the pocket corner of the 1873 work trouser.

materials.name: Platinum
materials.summary: A strong white metal that holds a thin setting; jewellers used it from about 1900 for lace-like settings of diamonds.

materials.name: Silver
materials.summary: A metal for mounts, spouts and rims of precious ware.

materials.name: Titanium
materials.summary: A light, strong metal; the first titanium watch case came in 1970, and jewellery and eyewear followed.

materials.name: Chrome (plated finish)
materials.summary: Bright chromium plate on brass or steel, the finish of taps and fittings after about 1925.

materials.name: Chrome plate
materials.summary: A thin bright layer of chromium on steel or brass; it made the brightwork of the car from the late 1920s.

materials.name: Gold-filled metal
materials.summary: A layer of gold alloy bonded to a base metal such as brass; the layer is much thicker than gold plate. Cheap pocket watch cases used it.

materials.name: Nickel plate
materials.summary: A thin layer of nickel on steel or brass. It gives a warm, slightly yellow shine and was the bright finish of cars before chrome.

materials.name: Ormolu (gilt bronze)
materials.summary: Fire-gilt bronze mounts that French dealers added to Chinese and Sèvres porcelain in the 18th century.

materials.name: Painted metal
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of matt black powder-coated steel

materials.name: Bare clay (unglazed)
materials.summary: No glaze: the fired clay is the surface. Bizen, Yixing, terracotta and jasper ware leave it bare.

materials.name: Biscuit (unglazed porcelain)
materials.summary: Fired porcelain left without glaze, matte and white like marble. Vincennes and Sèvres used it for figures.

materials.name: Burnished
materials.summary: Clay polished with a stone or a bone before firing, so that it shines without a glaze.

materials.name: Black basalt
materials.summary: A black unglazed stoneware coloured with iron and manganese, made for vases and teaware in the antique style.

materials.name: Bone china
materials.summary: A porcelain with calcined bone ash. It is white, thin and strong. Josiah Spode set the standard recipe about 1796.

materials.name: Ceramic tile
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of glazed ceramic tiles with grout

materials.name: Creamware
materials.summary: A cream-coloured earthenware with a lead glaze. Josiah Wedgwood refined it as Queen's ware in 1762.

materials.name: Earthenware
materials.summary: A porous body fired below about 1150 °C. Pots from Xianrendong Cave are the oldest known vessels of fired clay.

materials.name: Egyptian faience
materials.summary: A body of ground quartz with an alkaline flux that glazes itself when it dries and fires. It is not a clay body.

materials.name: European hard-paste porcelain
materials.summary: The first European true porcelain. The Meissen manufactory began production in 1710.

materials.name: Fireclay
materials.summary: A refractory clay that resists heat and holds a large cast without warping: Belfast sinks, baths and kiln furniture.

materials.name: Fired brick clay
materials.summary: A coarse clay fired in moulded blocks. Glazed brick makes the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, about 575 BC.

materials.name: Glass-ceramic
materials.summary: A glass that heat turns into a fine crystal ceramic, so that it takes a flame and the freezer. Stookey found it by accident; Corning Ware used it from 1958.

materials.name: Ironstone china
materials.summary: A hard, heavy, white body patented as a cheap substitute for porcelain.

materials.name: Jasperware
materials.summary: A fine unglazed stoneware coloured with metal oxides, with white relief in the same body.

materials.name: Paper clay
materials.summary: Clay mixed with paper fibre, so that thin sculptural forms stand and join when dry.

materials.name: Parian porcelain
materials.summary: An unglazed biscuit porcelain that looks like Parian marble. It made figures and busts for the Victorian home.

materials.name: Pearlware
materials.summary: Creamware with a little cobalt in the glaze, so that it looks whiter. It carries blue transfer prints well.

materials.name: Porcelain
materials.summary: A white, dense and translucent body of kaolin and porcelain stone, fired at about 1300 °C.

materials.name: Porcelain stoneware (gres porcellanato)
materials.summary: A pressed tile body with water absorption below 0.5 %. It makes floor and wall tiles that copy stone, wood and concrete.

materials.name: Pyrogranite
materials.summary: A hard, frost-proof architectural body that the Zsolnay factory developed. It makes roof tiles, relief panels and finials with a strong glaze.

materials.name: Raku clay
materials.summary: An open, grogged clay that survives the shock of a hot kiln. Pieces are hand-built, not thrown.

materials.name: Red stoneware (zisha)
materials.summary: A fine iron-rich stoneware, left unglazed. Yixing teapots in this body take a patina from tea.

materials.name: Soft-paste porcelain
materials.summary: A glassy body of white clay and frit, an early European imitation of Chinese porcelain. Sèvres used it until about 1770.

materials.name: Stonepaste (fritware)
materials.summary: A white body of ground quartz, glass frit and a little clay. Islamic potters used it to copy Chinese porcelain; Iznik ware uses it.

materials.name: Stoneware
materials.summary: A dense, vitrified body fired at about 1200 to 1300 °C. It holds water without a glaze.

materials.name: Technical porcelain
materials.summary: A high-alumina porcelain for electrical insulators and laboratory ware. It resists voltage, heat and acids.

materials.name: Terracotta
materials.summary: A red, iron-rich earthenware, often left unglazed. It makes figures, roof tiles and facade blocks.

materials.name: Vitreous china
materials.summary: A dense, white body with near zero water absorption, cast for sanitary ware: basins, WCs and urinals.

materials.name: Vitreous enamel
materials.summary: Glass fused onto metal; the dial of the fine watch and the colour of Art Nouveau and Art Deco jewels.

materials.name: Back-painted glass
materials.photo_applied: a square sample of a back-painted glass splashback

materials.name: Glass
materials.summary: A non-ceramic glassy material. It is a substitute that breaks the look of fired clay.

materials.name: Glass pearl
materials.summary: A glass bead coated with a pearl-like layer; the base of the long ropes of costume jewellery. By tradition, the rosary maker Jaquin made the first one in 1656.

materials.name: Paste
materials.summary: Lead glass cut and foil-backed to look like diamond; Georgian paste was a jewel of its own, not only a copy.

materials.name: Alkaline glaze
materials.summary: A glaze fluxed with soda or potash. It gives bright turquoise with copper and blue with cobalt.

materials.name: Ash glaze
materials.summary: A glaze from wood ash. In a wood kiln it forms by itself as green-brown runs on the shoulder of a pot.

materials.name: Celadon
materials.summary: A green to blue-green glaze from a little iron in reduction. Longquan and Korean Goryeo celadons are the classic forms.

materials.name: Clear porcelain glaze
materials.summary: A transparent high-fired feldspar glaze that shows the white body and underglaze painting.

materials.name: Coloured gloss glaze
materials.summary: A smooth, even, saturated industrial glaze in one colour.

materials.name: Copper red
materials.summary: A red glaze from copper in reduction, hard to control: sang de boeuf and flambé.

materials.name: Crackle glaze
materials.summary: A glaze that crazes in a net of lines on cooling. Potters stain the lines to show them.

materials.name: Crystalline glaze
materials.summary: A zinc glaze that grows flower-like crystals in a slow cool.

materials.name: Eosin glaze
materials.summary: An iridescent lustre glaze in red, purple and gold that the Zsolnay factory made. It gives roof finials and wall panels an oily metallic sheen.

materials.name: Iron brown glaze
materials.summary: A glossy brown glaze coloured by iron oxide. It covers telegraph and power insulators, because it hides soot and dirt and sheds rain.

materials.name: Jun glaze
materials.summary: A thick opalescent blue glaze, often with purple splashes of copper.

materials.name: Lava glaze
materials.summary: A thick, bubbled glaze that looks like lava, the surface of West German Fat Lava vases.

materials.name: Lead glaze
materials.summary: A clear, low-fired glaze fluxed with lead oxide. It is glossy and takes colour from metal oxides.

materials.name: Victorian majolica glaze
materials.summary: Bright coloured lead glazes over moulded relief, shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851.

materials.name: Matte glaze
materials.summary: A dry, velvet glaze. Grueby matte green set the surface of American art pottery.

materials.name: Oribe glaze
materials.summary: A copper-green glaze poured over part of a piece, named after the tea master Furuta Oribe.

materials.name: Raku glaze
materials.summary: A low-fired glaze on a piece pulled hot from the kiln. Black and red raku tea bowls are the canonical forms.

materials.name: Salt glaze
materials.summary: Salt thrown into a hot kiln forms a thin glaze with an orange-peel texture on stoneware.

materials.name: Sancai (three-colour)
materials.summary: Lead glazes in amber, green and cream that run together on tomb figures and vessels.

materials.name: Sanitary glaze
materials.summary: A glossy, hard, white zircon glaze that cleans easily, sprayed on vitreous china and fireclay.

materials.name: Satin glaze
materials.summary: A glaze between matte and gloss, about 20 to 50 GU, common on studio and Scandinavian ware.

materials.name: Shino glaze
materials.summary: A thick white feldspar glaze with pinholes and fire-orange edges.

materials.name: Soft-paste glaze
materials.summary: A soft, glassy lead glaze that fuses with the body of soft-paste porcelain. It pools in the corners and takes enamel colours well. English factories used it from about 1745.

materials.name: Tenmoku
materials.summary: A dark iron glaze that breaks to brown on rims. Hare's fur and oil spot are its effects.

materials.name: Tin glaze
materials.summary: An opaque white lead glaze with tin oxide. It is the base of maiolica, faience and delftware.

materials.name: Uranium oxide glaze
materials.summary: A bright orange-red glaze coloured with uranium oxide, the red of Fiesta ware.

materials.name: Albany slip
materials.summary: A natural brown clay from Albany, New York, that melts to a dark glossy coat at stoneware heat. American potters dipped crocks and jugs in it.

materials.name: Attic black gloss
materials.summary: A fine iron-rich slip that turns black and glossy in a three-stage firing. It makes black- and red-figure ware.

materials.name: Terra sigillata
materials.summary: A red gloss slip of very fine clay particles, the surface of Roman tableware.

materials.name: Technical ceramic
materials.summary: Zirconium oxide sintered hard and polished; it does not scratch and does not fade, and watch cases and bracelets use it.

materials.photo_applied: a square sample of glazed white wall tiles with grout

materials.photo_applied: a square sample of large porcelain floor tiles

materials.name: Polyurethane leatherette
materials.summary: A fabric with a polyurethane skin that is embossed to look like leather. Car makers use it for seats and trim in place of hide. DuPont launched the polyurethane leather substitute Corfam in 1963.

materials.name: PVC leathercloth
materials.summary: Plasticised PVC on a knit or woven back; the upholstery of the post-war car and the cheap handbag.

materials.name: ePTFE membrane laminate
materials.summary: A cloth laminated to a membrane of stretched PTFE with pores too small for water and large enough for vapour; first sold in garments in 1976.

materials.name: Neoprene
materials.summary: A foamed chloroprene rubber between knit faces; Hugh Bradner used it for the wetsuit in 1952, and fashion took it in the 2010s.

materials.name: Flash-spun polyethylene
materials.summary: A paper-like sheet of flash-spun fibre; designers use it for jackets and bags that look like envelopes.

materials.name: Microfibre suede
materials.summary: A nonwoven of very fine polyester in polyurethane that feels like suede; car cabins use it for seats and wheels.

materials.name: ABS plastic
materials.summary: A tough, mouldable plastic; one-piece injection-moulded watch cases used it from 1983.

materials.name: Cellulose acetate sheet
materials.summary: Plastic sheet cut and polished into eyeglass frames, with layers of colour and tortoiseshell patterns.

materials.name: Acrylic glass
materials.summary: A clear, light plastic; watches used it as a crystal that does not shatter, and handbags and jewellery used it in colour.

materials.name: Bakelite
materials.summary: The first fully synthetic plastic, a phenol-formaldehyde resin; cast Bakelite made the colourful bangles of the 1930s.

materials.name: Celluloid
materials.summary: The first thermoplastic, of nitrocellulose and camphor; it replaced ivory and tortoiseshell in combs, collars and frames.

materials.name: EVA foam
materials.summary: A light foam of ethylene-vinyl acetate for midsoles; it made the cushioned running shoe.

materials.name: Plastic
materials.summary: A moulded polymer, the usual substitute for ceramic in cheap ware.

materials.name: Polycarbonate
materials.summary: A clear, tough plastic. It replaced glass in lamp lenses and became a body panel material when moulded in large parts.

materials.name: Cellulose acetate
materials.summary: A cellulose fibre with a silk-like drape and lustre, used for linings and evening dress.

materials.name: Lyocell
materials.summary: A cellulose fibre spun from a solvent that the process recovers; it was sold from 1992.

materials.name: Viscose rayon
materials.summary: The first regenerated cellulose fibre made at scale; Chardonnet showed a nitrocellulose 'artificial silk' in 1889.

materials.name: Fluoroelastomer
materials.summary: A soft synthetic rubber that resists sweat, oil and sunlight. Smartwatch sport bands use it. DuPont launched the fluoroelastomer Viton in 1957.

materials.name: Vulcanised rubber
materials.summary: Rubber cured with sulphur so that it stays elastic; it made the galosh, the plimsoll and the sneaker sole.

materials.name: Acrylic
materials.summary: A synthetic fibre with a wool-like hand, used for knitwear and fleece.

materials.name: Aramid
materials.summary: A heat- and cut-resistant fibre with high strength, used for protective clothing and racing suits.

materials.name: Elastane
materials.summary: A polyurethane fibre that stretches to five or more times its length and recovers; it replaced rubber thread in foundation garments.

materials.name: Nylon
materials.summary: The first fully synthetic fibre; nylon stockings went on sale in 1940, and the war took the fibre for parachutes.

materials.name: Polyester
materials.summary: A synthetic fibre that holds a crease and a pleat; it became the fibre of easy-care dress in the 1950s and 1960s.

materials.name: Polypropylene
materials.summary: A light fibre that takes up almost no water; it became the first synthetic base layer in the 1970s.

materials.name: Synthetic insulation
materials.summary: Fine polyester fibre batting that keeps its warmth when wet; it replaced down in wet climates.

materials.name: Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene
materials.summary: A gel-spun fibre with a high strength for its weight, used in light technical packs and shells.

materials.name: Nylon mesh
materials.summary: An open warp-knit nylon that passes air and dries fast; the light upper of the running shoe, in place of leather and canvas.

materials.name: Nylon tricot
materials.summary: A fine warp-knit nylon with a smooth face and a run-resistant structure; the cloth of slips, briefs and linings.

materials.name: Powernet
materials.summary: A warp-knit elastic mesh for girdles, corsets and shapewear; it holds the body with no bones.

materials.name: Elastane jersey
materials.summary: A knit with elastane that fits the body with no darts; the cloth of swimwear, leggings and the body.

materials.name: Nylon sheer knit
materials.summary: The sheer knit of the nylon stocking; on its first day of sale in 1940 women bought about four million pairs.

materials.name: Polar fleece
materials.summary: A napped polyester knit made with Patagonia as a light, quick-dry replacement for wool pile; sold as Polartec from 1981.

materials.name: Recycled polyester knit
materials.summary: A knit made of polyester fibre that is spun from used plastic bottles. Car makers use it for seats and door trim.

materials.name: Velour
materials.summary: A soft knit with a cut pile. It covered the seats and door panels of many cars in the 1970s and 1980s.

materials.name: Ballistic nylon
materials.summary: A heavy basket-weave nylon made for flak jackets; it went into luggage, packs and watch straps.

materials.name: Ripstop nylon
materials.summary: A plain weave with a heavier yarn in a grid that stops a tear; made for parachutes, then shells and down jackets.

materials.name: Nylon webbing
materials.summary: A narrow, tough nylon tape. A British army standard of 1973 made it the one-piece watch strap that slides under the watch.

materials.name: Poly-cotton twill
materials.summary: A dense twill of about 65 per cent polyester and 35 per cent cotton that takes a wax finish; it was made for the Nordic field jacket and trouser.

materials.name: Concrete
materials.summary: A cast stone that replaced terracotta and faience on facades after about 1930.

materials.name: Carbon fibre
materials.summary: Carbon fibre in epoxy; a race car chassis used it in 1981, and watch cases and car trim use the woven look.

materials.name: Glass-reinforced plastic
materials.summary: Glass fibre in a resin; car bodies used it from 1953 for small series with curved panels.
