tools.name: Paintbrush
tools.summary: A handle with a tuft of hair or fibre that puts paint, glaze, slip or limewash on a surface.

tools.name: Burin
tools.summary: A steel cutter with a square or lozenge shaft that cuts lines into metal or wood.

tools.name: Chef's knife
tools.summary: A broad kitchen knife with a curved edge for slicing, dicing and mincing.

tools.name: Crucible
tools.summary: A heat-proof pot in which metal or glass melts before it is poured.

tools.name: Drawloom
tools.summary: A hand loom with a second set of cords that lift single warp threads, for figured silks.

tools.name: Electrolytic bath
tools.summary: A tank of metal-salt solution with two poles; a direct current moves metal from one pole onto the part.

tools.name: Etching press
tools.summary: A roller press with a steel bed and felt blankets that pushes damp paper into the grooves of an inked plate.

tools.name: Grill
tools.summary: A grate over glowing charcoal, wood or gas that cooks food with direct radiant heat.

tools.name: Hat block
tools.summary: A wooden form in the shape of a head or a crown, on which wet felt or straw is stretched and dried.

tools.name: Immersion circulator
tools.summary: A heater and pump that hold a water bath at a set temperature to within 0.1 °C.

tools.name: Injection moulding machine
tools.summary: A machine that melts plastic pellets and forces the melt into a closed steel mould.

tools.name: Kiln
tools.summary: A heat-proof chamber that fires clay, glaze, glass or enamel at 600 to 1400 °C.

tools.name: Loom
tools.summary: A frame that holds warp threads under tension so that weft threads can pass through them.

tools.name: Oven
tools.summary: A closed, heated chamber that cooks, dries or cures with hot air.

tools.name: Plaster mould
tools.summary: A mould of plaster of Paris that pulls water out of slip or soft clay, so that a skin of clay forms on its wall.

tools.name: Potter's wheel
tools.summary: A turning disc on which a potter throws, trims or bands a round pot.

tools.name: Printing press
tools.summary: A machine that presses inked type, a block or a stone onto paper or cloth.

tools.name: Rose engine lathe
tools.summary: A lathe whose head rocks against a cam, so that the cutter engraves repeated patterns (guilloché) in metal.

tools.name: Printing screen
tools.summary: A fine mesh on a frame with a stencil; a squeegee pushes ink through the open parts of the mesh.

tools.name: Smokehouse
tools.summary: A closed room or box in which food hangs in the smoke of a slow wood fire.

tools.name: Spit
tools.summary: A long rod that holds meat and turns it in front of or above a fire.

tools.name: Steamer
tools.summary: A basket of bamboo or metal with holes, over boiling water, that cooks food in the steam.

tools.name: Knitting frame
tools.summary: A machine with a row of needles that knits a flat, shaped panel of cloth.

tools.name: Timber formwork
tools.summary: A temporary mould of boards into which wet concrete is poured; the grain of the boards stays on the concrete.

tools.name: Welding torch
tools.summary: A torch or an arc electrode that melts the edges of two parts so that they join.

tools.name: Whipping siphon
tools.summary: A steel bottle that is filled with nitrous oxide and pushes a liquid out as a foam.

tools.name: Wok
tools.summary: A deep, round-bottomed steel pan for fast cooking over a very hot flame.

tools.name: Wood-fired kiln
tools.summary: A kiln with a firebox for wood; the ash in the flame settles on the pots and melts into a glaze.

processes.name: Cord-impressed
processes.note: Patterns pressed into wet clay with twisted cord, the mark that names Jōmon pottery.

processes.name: Incised and carved
processes.note: Lines cut or carved into the leather-hard clay, often under a glaze that pools in them.

processes.name: Black-figure painting
processes.note: Figures in black gloss slip on the red clay, with incised detail.

processes.name: Red-figure painting
processes.note: The ground is black gloss and the figures stay the red of the clay, drawn with a brush.

processes.name: Lustre
processes.note: A thin film of silver or copper fired in reduction on a glaze. It shines like metal.

processes.name: Sgraffito
processes.note: A line scratched through a slip to show the clay of another colour under it.

processes.name: Iron-oxide painting
processes.note: Brushwork in iron oxide that fires black or brown, under or over a glaze.

processes.name: Slip inlay
processes.note: Lines cut into the clay and filled with white and black slip, under a celadon glaze.

processes.name: Encaustic inlay
processes.note: A pattern of coloured clay inlaid into a tile, so that it does not wear off. Herbert Minton revived it in the 1830s.

processes.name: Cut-tile mosaic
processes.note: Glazed tiles cut into small shapes and set together in a geometric pattern.

processes.name: Underglaze cobalt blue
processes.note: Cobalt oxide painted on the raw body under a clear glaze: blue and white.

processes.name: Cuerda seca
processes.note: Coloured glazes held apart by a line of wax and manganese, so that they do not run together.

processes.name: Overglaze enamel
processes.note: Coloured glass enamels painted on a fired glaze and fixed in a low third firing. Jingdezhen used them on porcelain from the Chenghua reign (1465–1487).

processes.name: Istoriato painting
processes.note: Narrative scenes painted across the full surface of maiolica, after prints of paintings.

processes.name: Underglaze polychrome
processes.note: Several colours painted under a clear glaze, as on Iznik ware with its raised bole red.

processes.name: Kintsugi
processes.note: A repair of a broken piece with lacquer and gold dust, so that the break becomes a line of gold.

processes.name: Slip trailing
processes.note: Liquid slip trailed from a spout in lines and dots, as on English slipware.

processes.name: Famille rose enamel
processes.note: An opaque pink enamel of colloidal gold that adds soft shading to overglaze painting.

processes.name: Agateware and marbling
processes.note: Clays or slips of different colours mixed or combed, so that the pattern goes through the body.

processes.name: Transfer printing
processes.note: A pattern from an engraved copper plate printed on paper and moved to the ware. It made decoration cheap.

processes.name: Mocha dendritic
processes.note: A drop of acid colour on wet slip spreads into a pattern like a tree, on bands of turned ware.

processes.name: Sprigged relief
processes.note: Small relief motifs pressed in moulds and applied to the body, as on jasperware.

processes.name: Moulded relief
processes.note: Relief made in the mould with the piece itself.

processes.name: Pierced and reticulated
processes.note: Openwork cut through the wall of the piece.

processes.name: Gilding
processes.note: Gold fixed on the glaze in a low firing, then burnished or left bright.

processes.name: Liquid bright gold
processes.note: A gold resinate that fires bright without burnishing. It made gilding cheap.

processes.name: Spongeware
processes.note: Colour dabbed or stamped with a cut sponge, a cheap decoration for export ware.

processes.name: Pâte-sur-pâte
processes.note: Layers of white slip painted on a tinted body and carved, so that the relief looks translucent.

processes.name: Hand banding
processes.note: Lines of colour applied on a wheel at the rim and foot.

processes.name: Decal
processes.note: A printed transfer on a film that is slid onto the glaze and fired. It replaced hand transfer printing.

processes.name: Screen print
processes.note: A pattern printed through a mesh screen, used on tiles and tableware after about 1950.

processes.name: Digital inkjet print
processes.note: Ceramic inks printed by an inkjet head on tiles. It copies stone, wood and photographs.

processes.name: Wax resist
processes.note: Wax painted on the piece so that a glaze or slip does not take there.

processes.name: Cold-painted pigment
processes.note: Lacquer and mineral pigments painted on a fired body and not fired again. The Qin terracotta soldiers carried it, and Tang tomb figures used it for faces.

processes.name: Printed layer lines
processes.note: The fine horizontal ridges that a clay printer leaves as it builds a wall in layers of 1 to 2 mm. Digital ceramics keep them as the surface.

processes.name: Brushed white slip
processes.note: White slip swept over a dark stoneware body with a coarse brush, so that the strokes show (hakeme in Japanese). Joseon buncheong potters made it a main decoration.

processes.name: Stamped
processes.note: Small dies pressed into the leather-hard clay in rows (inhwa), then filled with white slip. Buncheong potters of the early Joseon court used it on dishes and bottles.

processes.name: Spit roasting
processes.note: Meat turned on a spit before an open fire; the roast of the medieval hall and the rôtisseur.

processes.name: Grilling
processes.note: Food cooked over glowing coals or a hot iron, with char lines.

processes.name: Wood-fire cooking
processes.note: Cooking in embers, ash and smoke; the open fire of the terroir kitchen.

processes.name: Oven roasting
processes.note: Roasting in a closed iron range; the range of the 1800s replaced the open hearth.

processes.name: Braising
processes.note: Meat browned and cooked slowly in a little liquid under a lid.

processes.name: Poaching
processes.note: Cooking in liquid just under the boil: fish in court-bouillon, eggs, fruit.

processes.name: Steaming
processes.note: Cooking in steam over boiling water; the light method of China and of cuisine minceur.

processes.name: Boiling
processes.note: Cooking in boiling liquid; pottery of about 20,000 years ago shows it.

processes.name: Sautéing
processes.note: Quick cooking in a little fat in a wide pan, with the pan moved by the cook.

processes.name: Deep frying
processes.note: Food dropped into hot fat; tempura reached Japan from the Portuguese in the 1500s.

processes.name: Confit
processes.note: Meat cooked slowly in its own fat and kept under it.

processes.name: Stock (fond)
processes.note: Bones, vegetables and herbs simmered for hours; the fonds of the French kitchen.

processes.name: Roux
processes.note: Flour cooked in fat; it thickens sauces and replaced bread as the thickener.

processes.name: Mother sauces
processes.note: A system of base sauces from which each other sauce comes; Escoffier fixed the five in 1903.

processes.name: Emulsion sauce
processes.note: Butter or oil held in egg yolk or a reduction: hollandaise, béarnaise, mayonnaise, beurre blanc.

processes.name: Reduction
processes.note: A liquid boiled down to concentrate its taste and to thicken it, without flour.

processes.name: Bread thickening
processes.note: Sauces of the medieval court thickened with soaked bread, ground almonds or liver.

processes.name: Larding
processes.note: Strips of fat threaded through lean meat with a needle before it is roasted.

processes.name: Aspic and chaud-froid
processes.note: Meat or fish set in a clear jelly of stock; the cold buffet of the grand kitchen.

processes.name: Pâté en croûte
processes.note: Meat baked in a pastry case; the pie of the medieval and classic feast.

processes.name: Knife work
processes.note: Exact cuts: julienne, brunoise, tournée and chiffonade; in Japan the work of the itamae.

processes.name: Plating in the kitchen
processes.note: The chef arranges each plate in the kitchen and the waiter only carries it; nouvelle cuisine made this the norm.

processes.name: Sous vide
processes.note: Food sealed in plastic and cooked in water at an exact low temperature; first for foie gras.

processes.name: Spherification
processes.note: A liquid set in a skin of alginate gel in a calcium bath; it bursts in the mouth.

processes.name: Siphon foam
processes.note: A purée or a liquid aerated with nitrous oxide in a cream siphon: the espuma.

processes.name: Liquid nitrogen freezing
processes.note: Instant freezing at minus 196 °C. In 1901 Marshall proposed liquid air for ice cream at the table; modernist chefs used liquid nitrogen after 1990.

processes.name: Dehydrating
processes.note: Water taken out with dry air or low heat; leathers, crisps and powders.

processes.name: Smoking
processes.note: Food exposed to the smoke of wood or hay; cold smoke cures, hot smoke cooks.

processes.name: Salt curing
processes.note: Salt draws water out of fish and meat: gravlaks, ham, salt cod.

processes.name: Pickling
processes.note: Food kept in vinegar or brine.

processes.name: Lacto-fermentation
processes.note: Lactic bacteria sour vegetables in salt: sauerkraut, kimchi, fermented juices.

processes.name: Koji fermentation
processes.note: The mould Aspergillus oryzae grown on rice or barley makes miso, soy sauce and sake; the Nordic kitchen took it up after 2010.

processes.name: Acid curing
processes.note: Raw fish turned firm and opaque by lime juice in minutes: the cure of ceviche.

processes.name: Raw slicing
processes.note: Raw fish and meat cut to show their grain: sashimi, carpaccio, crudo. The word sashimi is first written in a diary of 1399.

processes.name: Wok cooking
processes.note: Stir-frying in a thin iron pan over high flame, for wok hei, the breath of the wok.

processes.name: Indigo-dyed
processes.note: A blue from the indigo plant; it sits on the surface of the yarn and fades with wear, the colour of denim.

processes.name: Aniline-dyed
processes.note: Coal-tar dyes from Perkin's mauveine; they gave the strong violets, magentas and greens of the 1860s.

processes.name: Mercerised
processes.note: Cotton treated with caustic soda; under tension (Horace Lowe, 1890) it takes a silk-like lustre and a deeper dye.

processes.name: Sanforised
processes.note: A cloth shrunk in the mill so that a garment keeps its size after a wash; it fixed the size of jeans and shirts.

processes.name: Napped
processes.note: Fibres raised from the surface with teasels or wire; flannel, fleece and the face of suede.

processes.name: Fulled
processes.note: Wool cloth beaten and wetted until the fibres mat and the cloth shrinks and thickens; loden and melton.

processes.name: Wax-proofed
processes.note: A paraffin or beeswax dressing that sheds water and darkens with wear; it needs a new dressing each year.

processes.name: Water-repellent coated
processes.note: A thin chemical finish that beads water on the face of a shell or a coat; the industry now moves to fluorine-free types.

processes.name: Stonewashed
processes.note: Garments tumbled with pumice for a soft hand and a pale, uneven indigo; the denim of the 1980s.

processes.name: Block-printed
processes.note: Colour pressed on with carved wood blocks, one block for each colour; the method of Indian calico and of the Arts and Crafts.

processes.name: Roller-printed
processes.note: Colour printed from engraved copper rollers at speed; it made printed cotton a cheap fashion.

processes.name: Screen-printed
processes.note: Colour pushed through a stencil on a mesh; the method of the printed T-shirt and the large silk-scarf design. Samuel Simon patented the method in 1907.

processes.name: Embroidered
processes.note: Pattern stitched into the cloth with a needle, in silk, wool, metal thread or beads.

processes.name: Beaded and sequinned
processes.note: Beads, sequins and paillettes sewn onto the cloth; the evening dress of the 1920s and of red-carpet couture.

processes.name: Quilted
processes.note: Two layers stitched through a fill in a grid of lines or channels; the down jacket and the chain-strap handbag. An ivory figure of a king in a quilted cloak is from about 3400 BC.

processes.name: Heat-set pleated
processes.note: Pleats fixed with heat in silk or polyester; Fortuny's Delphos gown and the pleated garments of the 1990s.

processes.name: Glazed
processes.note: Cloth pressed hot with starch or resin for a shine; the finish of chintz.

processes.name: Burnished
processes.note: Leather rubbed with wax and heat until the toe and heel go dark and glossy; the finish of the dress shoe.

processes.name: Patent-lacquered
processes.note: A hard lacquer at 80 GU and more; patent shoes, belts and bags. Seth Boyden made the first patent leather in 1818.

processes.name: Distressed
processes.note: Wear made on purpose: abrasion, rips, fades and creases.

processes.name: Polished
processes.note: A mirror surface at 80 GU and more on metal, gem, plastic or lacquered wood.

processes.name: Brushed
processes.note: Fine parallel lines from an abrasive that give a satin sheen; the case flank of a sports watch.

processes.name: Guilloché
processes.note: A fine engine-turned pattern cut on a rose engine. Breguet put it on watch dials from about 1786.

processes.name: Engraved
processes.note: Lines cut by hand with a graver; the case back of a pocket watch and the shank of a ring.

processes.name: Enamelled
processes.note: Glass fused into or onto metal: champlevé, cloisonné, plique-à-jour or painted.

processes.name: Gilded
processes.note: A thin layer of gold leaf or electroplate on base metal, leather edges or wood.

processes.name: Rhodium-plated
processes.note: A thin bright white layer on white gold or silver that does not tarnish.

processes.name: PVD-coated
processes.note: A thin hard film by physical vapour deposition, black or coloured, on steel cases and bracelets.

processes.name: Faceted
processes.note: Flat facets cut to return light; the round brilliant cut has 57 or 58 facets.

processes.name: Cabochon
processes.note: A smooth domed stone with no facets; the oldest gem cut and the crown of a Cartier watch.

processes.name: Gloss paint
processes.note: Body paint at 80 GU and more, solid or two-tone; the finish of the car body.

processes.name: Metallic paint
processes.note: Body paint with aluminium flake that sparkles in the light.

processes.name: Woven leather
processes.note: Thin strips of leather woven by hand into a plain weave; the 'intrecciato' of Italian leather goods.

processes.name: Tie-dyed
processes.note: Cloth that is tied, folded or bound before the dye bath, so that the bound parts resist the dye; Japanese shibori is an old form, and American dress took it up in the 1960s.

processes.name: Studded
processes.note: Metal studs or spikes fixed through cloth or leather; the biker jacket carried them, and punk dress made them a mark of the style.

processes.name: Coated
processes.note: A cloth or hide covered in lacquer or resin so that it sheds rain and shows a printed pattern; the grey lacquered canvas of the first flat-topped trunk is an early case.

processes.name: Seam-taped
processes.note: A heat-sealed strip over each needle line, so that rain cannot pass the stitch holes; the mark of a membrane shell.

processes.name: Garment-dyed
processes.note: A garment that is dyed after it is sewn, in a drum; it gives one colour over the cloth, the thread and the tape.

processes.name: Foiled
processes.note: A thin metal foil behind a stone or a paste to raise its colour and brilliance; common in Georgian jewellery.

processes.name: Pierced
processes.note: Openwork cut with a saw; the pierced frame lets light pass and lowers the weight of the metal.

processes.name: Carved
processes.note: Material cut away by hand or by tool to make a relief, a cameo or a figure.

processes.name: Plique-a-jour
processes.note: Enamel set in open cells with no backing, so that light passes through like stained glass.

processes.name: Hammered
processes.note: Metal marked with hammer blows; the dents show the hand of the maker and break the light.

processes.name: Oxidised
processes.note: A dark film made on silver or copper by a chemical bath; it sits in the recesses and shows the relief.

processes.name: Milgrained
processes.note: A row of tiny beads cut along an edge of metal; it gives a fine, lace-like border.

processes.name: Electroplated
processes.note: A thin layer of gold, silver or chrome put on a base metal by an electric bath.

processes.name: Anodised
processes.note: An oxide layer grown on aluminium in an acid bath. It takes dye and gives a hard, matt, coloured surface.

processes.name: Moulded
processes.note: Shaped in a mould under heat or pressure, so that the part leaves the mould with its final form.

processes.name: Architectural faience
processes.note: A hollow slab of fine clay with a coloured glaze on the visible face. It clads a wall with a bright, washable skin.

processes.name: Ash glazing
processes.note: A glaze that comes from wood or plant ash. The ash melts with the clay and makes a green, yellow or brown glass.

processes.name: Board-marked concrete
processes.note: Concrete cast in rough timber forms, so that the grain and the joints of the boards stay on the surface.

processes.name: Bone-ash body
processes.note: A porcelain body that holds calcined bone ash, about 40 to 50 per cent, with china clay and china stone. It fires white and strong at a lower heat.

sources.title: Edward Durell Stone, United States Embassy, New Delhi (1959)

processes.name: Breeze block
processes.note: A hollow concrete block with a pierced pattern; a wall of them shades and lets air and light through.

sources.title: Rosemary Crill, Chintz: Indian Textiles for the West (2008)

processes.name: Chintz
processes.note: Cotton printed with large flowers and birds, often glazed, used for curtains, covers and walls.

processes.name: Coated canvas
processes.note: Cotton or linen canvas covered with lacquer, paint or resin, so that it sheds rain, wipes clean and takes a printed pattern.

processes.name: Elastic gusset
processes.note: A side panel of rubber webbing set into the shaft of a boot, so that the boot slips on without laces or buttons.

processes.name: Glazed roof tile
processes.note: A roof tile of fine clay with a coloured lead glaze. The glaze makes the roof bright, hard and watertight, and its colour shows the rank of the building.

processes.name: Gold pink enamel
processes.note: A soft rose-pink overglaze enamel that colloidal gold makes. Painters mix it with white enamel to make a range of tints from deep rose to white.

processes.name: Laminated timber
processes.note: Thin boards or veneers glued in layers, so that wood forms long spans, bent shapes and large panels.

processes.name: Lastex yarn
processes.note: An elastic yarn with a rubber core wrapped in wool, rayon, silk or cotton thread; it let a knitted garment stretch and return.

processes.name: Lava glazing
processes.note: A thick glaze that blisters and runs in the kiln. It leaves a rough, cratered surface like cooled lava, often in two or more colours.

processes.name: Limewash
processes.note: A thin wash of slaked lime that dries to a soft, matt white with a faint cloud of brush marks.

processes.name: Matt glazing
processes.note: A thick, dry-looking glaze with a velvet surface. The potter adds alumina or a silica surplus, so that fine crystals make the surface dull.

processes.name: Membrane lamination
processes.note: A thin membrane with pores that block water drops. Pass water vapour, bonded between a face cloth and a liner to make a shell cloth.

processes.name: Neon glow
processes.note: Light as a line of coloured gas, with a soft halo that spills onto the dark ground around it.

processes.name: Polar fleece knit
processes.note: A napped polyester knit that is light, dries fast and keeps its loft when wet; it replaced wool pile as the mid layer.

processes.name: PVC-coated cloth
processes.note: A woven or knit cloth that is coated with plasticised PVC, so that it is shiny, waterproof and easy to wipe clean.

processes.name: Pyrogranite tile
processes.note: A hard, frost-proof ceramic that the Zsolnay factory made from 1886. It is fired at a very high heat and carries a strong glaze, so that it can face roofs and walls.

processes.name: Raised bole red
processes.note: A thick slip of red clay that stands in low relief on the tile and fires to a bright tomato red under a clear glaze. It is the signature colour of Iznik tiles.

processes.name: Rubber vulcanisation
processes.note: The heating of rubber with sulphur, so that it stays elastic in heat and cold. It made the rubber sole.

sources.title: Lawrence Lee, George Seddon and Francis Stephens, Stained Glass (1976)

processes.name: Stained glass
processes.note: Pieces of coloured glass held in lead strips, so that a window becomes a picture of coloured light.

processes.name: Stonepaste body
processes.note: A body of ground quartz, glass frit and a little white clay. It is white and hard, and it takes a thin glaze, but it is not as clear as porcelain.

processes.name: Tenmoku iron glaze
processes.note: A thick glaze with a high share of iron oxide. In a reduction firing the iron forms streaks, spots and a dark, glassy body.

sources.title: Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus, entry: terrazzo

processes.name: Terrazzo
processes.note: Chips of marble or glass set in a binder and ground flat, so that each chip shows as a cut section.

processes.name: Uranium oxide glazing
processes.note: A lead glaze that holds uranium oxide fires to a bright orange-red. The red cannot be made with the common metal oxides at that heat.

processes.name: Vitreous enamelling
processes.note: A thin coat of glass that is fused to iron or steel at about 800 °C. It makes a hard, bright, washable surface that resists heat and rust.

processes.name: Layered plastic frame
processes.note: A spectacle frame cut and polished from sheets of celluloid or acetate, often two or more layers of colour glued together before cutting.

processes.name: Automotive clay modelling
processes.note: A designer shapes a full-size car in warm industrial clay over a frame. The clay is cut, smoothed and checked in light before any metal is made.

processes.name: Box-baffle quilt
processes.note: A quilt with a wall of cloth between the two faces of each cell. Loose down stays in its place and gives even warmth.

processes.name: Boning
processes.note: A way to stiffen a bodice with thin strips of whalebone, cane or steel set in narrow channels, so that the cloth holds the shape of the torso.

processes.name: Bread-thickened sauce
processes.note: A sauce that a cook binds with soaked and strained bread. The sauce gets body and a soft texture, and it carries spice and acid.

processes.name: Broken tile mosaic
processes.note: A mosaic of shards of glazed tile and china set in mortar. A mason can cover a curved surface with it, and the pieces give free, bright colour.

processes.name: Ceramic rainscreen
processes.note: A wall skin of hollow clay panels on rails, with an air gap behind. The panels keep rain off the wall, and the air dries it.

processes.name: Ceramming
processes.note: A formed piece of glass is heated in two steps. Fine crystals grow in the glass and make it a glass-ceramic that does not break in a heat shock.

processes.name: Ceviche curing
processes.note: Raw fish stays in lime juice with salt and chilli for a few minutes, until the surface turns firm and opaque, and is served at once with its juice.

processes.name: Chrome plating
processes.note: A thin layer of chromium is put on steel by electrolysis. The layer gives a hard, bright surface that does not tarnish.

processes.name: Cobalt underglaze painting
processes.note: Cobalt oxide is painted on the raw or bisque body. A clear glaze covers it, and one firing turns the paint a deep blue.

processes.name: Copper rivet reinforcement
processes.note: A small copper rivet set at a point of strain, such as a pocket corner or the base of a fly. The seam does not tear.

processes.name: Cord marking
processes.note: Twisted cord or a cord-wrapped stick is rolled or pressed into the wet clay wall. It leaves a dense texture of fine ridges.

processes.name: Cuerda seca
processes.note: A line of grease and manganese oxide is drawn round each colour field on an unfired tile, so that the coloured glazes do not run into each other. The line fires to a matt dark edge.

processes.name: Cut tile mosaic
processes.note: Glazed tiles of one colour are cut into small shapes, and the shapes are set face down in a plaster bed to form a pattern. The bed holds the pieces after it dries.

processes.name: Dust pressing
processes.note: Nearly dry clay powder is pressed in a steel die under high pressure to form a tile in one step. The tile needs little drying and keeps its size.

processes.name: Etching
processes.note: An intaglio print from a metal plate whose lines a needle draws through an acid-resistant ground and an acid then bites.

processes.name: Exposed joinery
processes.note: A joint that stays in view, so that the way of making is part of the look.

processes.name: Figured silk weaving
processes.note: The weaving of patterns into silk cloth on a draw loom, so that flowers and ribbons appear in the weave of the cloth.

processes.name: Flourless reduction sauce
processes.note: A sauce made from the cooking juices and a stock, reduced and finished with a little cream, butter, fromage blanc or a vegetable purée, with no flour roux.

processes.name: Fully fashioned knitting
processes.note: A way to knit each part of a garment to shape, and then to join the parts by linking stitch to stitch, so that the seam is flat.

processes.name: Garment dyeing
processes.note: A garment is dyed after it is sewn, in a drum. Cloth, thread and tape take one colour and each piece differs a little.

processes.name: Garment pleating
processes.note: A way to pleat cloth after the garment is cut and sewn, with a heat press, so that the pleats stay for good.

processes.name: Glass-fibre moulding
processes.note: Glass-fibre mat is laid in a mould and wet with resin. The resin sets and leaves a light, rust-free shell.

processes.name: Glaze splashing
processes.note: Lead glazes of different colours are brushed, dripped or splashed on a fired body. They run together in the second firing and make streaks of amber, green and cream.

processes.name: Glazed brick relief
processes.note: Bricks are pressed in a relief mould, glazed in colour and fired, then laid in numbered courses so that the figures form on the wall.

processes.name: Goodyear welting
processes.note: A way to sew a strip of leather, the welt, to the upper and the insole rib, and then to stitch the sole to the welt.

processes.name: Hat blocking
processes.note: A milliner steams a felt or straw hat body and pulls it over a carved wooden block, so that it dries in the shape of the crown and the brim.

processes.name: Hollow terracotta block
processes.note: A building block of clay that has webs inside. A maker presses it in a mould, so that it dries and fires without a crack and weighs little.

processes.name: Injection moulding
processes.note: Hot plastic is pushed into a steel mould under high pressure. The part cools, and the mould opens to release it.

processes.name: Interchangeable parts watchmaking
processes.note: A factory method in which machines cut every part to a gauge, so that a part from one watch fits any other watch of the same model.

processes.name: Inverted firing
processes.note: A bowl is fired upside down on its rim in a ring of fireclay, so that the wall stays thin and true. The rim has no glaze and takes a metal band.

processes.name: Joined-hemisphere throwing
processes.note: Two large bowls are thrown on the wheel and joined at the rim when leather-hard. The seam is smoothed, and the sphere closes at the top with a collar.

processes.name: Lacto-fermentation
processes.note: Vegetables in a salt brine are soured by lactic bacteria; the acid and the savoury taste keep the food and add depth to a dish.

processes.name: Layered glazing
processes.note: A glaze is put on in several thin coats with a firing or a drying step between them. The layers make a thick, deep and soft surface.

processes.name: Lost-wax casting
processes.note: A method that melts a wax model out of a mould and fills the empty space with molten metal.

processes.name: Lustre firing
processes.note: A thin film of copper or silver on a glazed pot gives a metallic shine. The potter paints a pigment on the glaze and fires it in smoke at a low heat.

processes.name: Lustre painting
processes.note: A paint with copper and silver salts is brushed on a glazed pot. A second firing in a smoky kiln leaves a thin layer of metal with a gold or copper shine.

processes.name: Overglaze enamelling
processes.note: Coloured glass enamels are painted on a glazed and fired piece. A third firing at a low heat fixes them on the glaze.

processes.name: Platform sole
processes.note: A sole that is raised under the whole foot by layers of cork, wood or foam, and that is covered in leather or cloth.

processes.name: Platinum mounting
processes.note: A frame of platinum, a metal strong enough to hold stones with thin lines, so that the metal nearly disappears.

processes.name: Pounce transfer
processes.note: A drawing on paper is pricked along its lines and dabbed with a bag of charcoal dust, so that dots of the design go onto the surface below.

processes.name: Press moulding in a bowl mould
processes.note: Soft clay is pressed into a fired clay mould that carries a design in reverse. The bowl keeps a sharp relief when it comes out of the mould.

processes.name: Raku firing
processes.note: A short, hot firing of one small piece. The potter opens the kiln and pulls the glowing piece out with tongs.

processes.name: Reduction firing
processes.note: A kiln fires with too little air, so that the flames take oxygen from the glaze and the clay. Iron turns green or black, and copper turns red.

processes.name: Salt glazing
processes.note: Rock salt is thrown into a kiln at stoneware heat. The salt vapour reacts with the clay and forms a thin hard glaze with an orange-peel texture.

processes.name: Sanggam inlay
processes.note: Lines are cut into leather-hard clay and filled with white or black slip. The glaze then covers the surface, and the pattern shows below it.

processes.name: Screen printing
processes.note: Ink pushed through a fine mesh with a squeegee; a stencil on the mesh blocks the parts that do not print.

processes.name: Sheet-metal pressing
processes.note: A press forms a flat steel sheet into a body panel in one stroke. The panels are then welded into a body.

processes.name: Slip casting
processes.note: Liquid clay is poured into a plaster mould. The plaster takes water from the clay and a wall forms on the inside of the mould.

processes.name: Slip trailing
processes.note: Liquid clay, called slip, is trailed from a quill or a pipe onto the leather-hard pot in lines and dots. The lines stay raised under the glaze.

processes.name: Soak-stain
processes.note: Thin paint is poured on raw, unprimed canvas that lies on the floor; the cloth drinks the colour and the colour and the weave become one.

processes.name: Sous vide
processes.note: Food is sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath at an exact low temperature, so that the whole piece reaches the same core heat.

processes.name: Spherification
processes.note: A liquid dropped into a calcium bath forms a thin skin of alginate gel; the sphere holds its shape on the spoon and bursts in the mouth.

processes.name: Sponge stamping
processes.note: A piece of sea sponge is dipped in ceramic colour and dabbed or stamped on a biscuit pot. The soft print is quick and needs little skill.

processes.name: Sprig moulding
processes.note: A small relief is pressed in a mould of fired clay, lifted out and fixed to the damp body with water. Potters use it to add figures and leaves.

processes.name: Three-stage firing
processes.note: One firing in three stages turns a slip black and leaves the clay red. Air is let in, shut out, and let in again.

processes.name: Thrown and assembled form
processes.note: A potter throws two or more separate parts and joins them at the leather-hard stage. The joined form has a shape that no single throw can make.

processes.name: Tie-dye
processes.note: A way to colour cloth in which parts are tied, folded or bound before the dye bath, so that the bound parts resist the dye.

processes.name: Tin glazing
processes.note: A pot is dipped in a glaze with tin oxide in it. The glaze dries to a white, opaque coat on which a potter paints with oxides before the glaze firing.

processes.name: Transfer printing
processes.note: A design is engraved on a copper plate, printed on thin paper in a ceramic ink and moved from the paper to the glazed or biscuit piece.

processes.name: Underglaze transfer printing
processes.note: A pattern is printed from an engraved copper plate on thin paper. The paper is rubbed on to the biscuit ware and the glaze covers the print.

processes.name: Wax proofing
processes.note: A dressing of oil or wax worked into a dense cloth so that it sheds water; the owner renews it each year.

processes.name: Wire work
processes.note: Actors hang on thin steel wires, so that they fly, leap and turn in a fight faster and higher than a body can.

processes.name: Wood type
processes.note: Large display letters routed from end-grain wood instead of cast in metal, so posters and bills can use letters 5–50 cm high at a low cost.

processes.name: Woodcut
processes.note: A print from a block of wood with the white parts cut away; the result is flat colour, hard edges and visible grain.

processes.name: Letterpress
processes.note: Printing from raised metal or wood type and blocks, locked in a forme and pressed into the paper.

sources.title: Alexander Lawson, Anatomy of a Typeface (Godine, 1990)

processes.name: Line engraving
processes.note: Lines cut into a metal plate with a burin; thin hairlines and swelling strokes give tone, and the print keeps a sharp, even edge.

processes.name: Mezzotint
processes.note: An intaglio tone process: a rocker roughens the whole plate to a black, and the engraver scrapes and burnishes the lights.

processes.name: Lithography
processes.note: A print from a flat stone or plate on which a greasy drawing takes ink and water repels it; the artist draws as on paper.

processes.name: Tweed weaving
processes.note: A rough woollen twill, woven from yarn that is dyed in the wool. A check or a heather mix that comes from the fleck of colours.

processes.name: Yarn proofing
processes.note: A rain cloth made from yarn that is proofed before it is woven, so that the cloth sheds water and the body can still breathe.

processes.name: Bias cutting
processes.note: The cutting of woven cloth at 45 degrees to the threads, so that it stretches, falls in soft folds and follows the body.

processes.name: Couture beading
processes.note: Beads and sequins are sewn by hand on a cloth, one by one or in a chain, in rows that make a dense, glittering surface.

processes.name: Cut steel work
processes.note: Small steel studs with many facets, riveted to a plate. They catch the light like diamonds and cost far less.

processes.name: Engine turning
processes.note: A lathe with a cutting tool cuts a regular pattern of fine lines in a flat metal face. The pattern catches the light and shows no tool marks.

processes.name: Hand building
processes.note: A vessel or a figure is built from coils, slabs or pinched lumps of clay, with no wheel. The maker joins the parts with slip and keeps the marks of the hand.

processes.name: Hand-canvassed tailoring
processes.note: The tailor builds the chest of a coat from layers of hair canvas, shaped and stitched by hand, so that the coat holds its roll and fits the body.

processes.name: Jet carving
processes.note: The cutting and polishing of jet, a hard black fossil wood, into beads, brooches and cameos.

processes.name: Pochoir
processes.note: Colour put on by hand through a set of cut stencils, one for each colour, over a printed key line.

processes.name: Saddle stitch
processes.note: A hand stitch in which one thread with a needle at each end passes twice through each hole; if one stitch breaks, the seam holds.

processes.name: Sugar sculpture
processes.note: A table piece that a cook models from sugar paste, marzipan and pastry in the shape of a building or a beast. It shows the wealth and skill of the host.

processes.name: Tambour embroidery
processes.note: A fast chain stitch made with a fine hook on cloth that is stretched tight in a frame; later the same hook sews beads on silk.

processes.name: Toile fitting
processes.note: A trial garment in plain calico, fitted and pinned on the client or on a stand before the real cloth is cut.

processes.name: Zisha slab building
processes.note: A hand method to build a thin-walled teapot from beaten slabs and strips of zisha clay, with no wheel and no mould.

processes.name: Thrown-form alteration
processes.note: A potter throws a plain vessel on the wheel and then bends, pinches, cuts and joins it while it is wet, so that the vessel becomes an animal or a figure.

processes.name: Coachbuilding
processes.note: The making of a car body by hand on a wood frame, and the fit of that body to a chassis that the client bought.

processes.name: Welding
processes.note: Two parts of metal or thermoplastic are joined: heat melts the edges, and the melt sets into one piece. The seam can show, or be ground away.

processes.name: Electroplating
processes.note: An electric current puts a thin layer of one metal on a part of another metal. Silver, gold, nickel and chromium plate give a cheap base metal a precious or hard surface.
